c.tagline: Cambodia's beach-and-casino boomtown, launchpad to the islands of Koh Rong.

taxi.fareNote: There is no metered street-taxi fleet; get around by tuk-tuk or car booked through the Grab or PassApp apps, which show an upfront fixed fare. Street tuk-tuks and motos have no meter, so agree the price first. US dollars are used everywhere alongside riel, with change under a dollar given in riel.

emergency.note: 119 reaches an ambulance and 118 the fire service, but response can be slow; the Tourist Police handle visitor issues and private hospitals often dispatch their own ambulances faster. Petty and organized crime rose sharply during the casino boom, so take extra care at night.

avoid.reason: Rapid casino-driven change — construction, scams and crime have risen; caution at night

hood_desc: The heart of Sihanoukville's beach tourism, a strip of sand backed by bars, seafood shacks, hostels and the ferry pier for the islands; busy and nightlife-heavy and where most first-timers land, though casino towers now loom behind it.
A longer, quieter stretch of sand south of the center split into Otres 1 and 2, with mellow beach bars, bungalows and yoga; the go-to for travelers wanting the old laid-back Sihanoukville feel.

The commercial center inland from the beaches along Ekareach Street, with the Psar Leu market, banks, the bus stations and the deep-water port; practical rather than pretty, and central for onward transport.
An older nightlife and guesthouse quarter on the hill above Victory Beach, once the backpacker core, now a mix of bars, budget rooms and Chinese businesses near the port.
A calmer resort stretch of coast around Independence and Sokha beaches west of downtown, home to landmark hotels and quieter sands; suits travelers wanting resort comfort away from the party strip.

water.note: Drink bottled or filtered water only.

transit.pay: Tuk-tuks and motos are hailed on the street or booked on PassApp/Grab, paid in cash (US dollars or riel) or in-app; there is no city transit card. Agree street fares before you set off.
transit.hours: Tuk-tuks and ride apps operate through the day and late into the night around the beach strip.
transit.note: Sihanoukville has no metro, tram, or urban rail and only minimal local bus service. Tuk-tuks (hailed or booked on PassApp/Grab) are how nearly everyone gets around; intercity coaches and the Royal Railway link to Phnom Penh.

bus: Long-distance coaches (Giant Ibis, Virak Buntham) to Phnom Penh, Kampot and Siem Reap
ferry: Fast ferries to Koh Rong and Koh Rong Sanloem (Speed Ferry Cambodia, Buva Sea)

transit.m: Grab/PassApp car to the beaches (30-40 min)

tip.r: Not customary; rounding up or leaving 5-10% at tourist restaurants and for tuk-tuk drivers is appreciated but never expected.

landmarks: Koh Rong
Cambodia's celebrated island escape offshore from Sihanoukville, ringed by squeaky white beaches, turquoise water and glowing bioluminescent plankton after dark.
Koh Rong Sanloem
Koh Rong's quieter sister island, where the perfect crescent of Saracen Bay and sleepy Lazy Beach define barefoot bliss.
Ream National Park
A coastal park of mangrove estuaries, jungle trails and empty beaches east of the city, explored by boat along the Prek Toek Sap River.
Wat Leu (Upper Pagoda)
A hilltop Buddhist temple on Sihanoukville Mountain offering sweeping views over the city, port and island-dotted gulf.
Wat Krom (Lower Pagoda)
An ornate seaside temple dedicated to the protective spirit Yeay Mao, its colourful shrines and naga staircases busy with local worshippers.
Ochheuteal Beach
The city's long main beach strip of casuarina trees and seafood shacks, its northern Serendipity end long the hub of traveller life.
Otres Beach
A more laid-back ribbon of pale sand south of town, known for mellow beach bars, calm swimming and blazing sunsets.
Independence Beach
A quiet palm-backed beach named for the landmark 1960s Independence Hotel, with clear water and fewer crowds than Ochheuteal.
Kbal Chhay Waterfalls
A multi-tiered cascade in the forest north of Sihanoukville, a favourite local picnic spot that thunders impressively in the rainy season.
Sokha Beach
Arguably Sihanoukville's prettiest in-town beach, a kilometre of fine white sand fronting the landmark Sokha resort, publicly accessible at one end.

train.note: The station is about 2.5 km north of the centre, so allow for a tuk-tuk at either end. Passenger trains run on the southern line to Phnom Penh via Kampot and Takeo roughly four times a week, taking about 7 hours - slower than the bus but scenic and by far the most relaxed way to travel, and it is the only stretch of Cambodian railway with a reliable timetable. Tickets are sold at the station and through BookMeBus (https://www.bookmebus.com/) and the train is often busy at weekends. There are no international trains from Cambodia; the port line here is otherwise a freight artery serving Sihanoukville Autonomous Port.

intl.to: Bangkok & Trat (Thailand) - via the Cham Yeam / Hat Lek border at Koh Kong, about 5 hr to the frontier
intl.op: Virak Buntham Express, Rith Mony & Bun Thou

intl.to: Ha Tien & Ho Chi Minh City (Vietnam) - via the Prek Chak / Xa Xia border, 10-12 hr

bus.note: Buses use operator offices rather than one terminal, mostly along Ekareach Street and around the Golden Lions roundabout; Phnom Penh Sorya, GST and Mekong Express run to Phnom Penh roughly hourly (3-5 hours, US$4.50-10) and Giant Ibis (https://www.giantibis.com/) has the most comfortable service. For Thailand the minibuses run to the Koh Kong crossing at Cham Yeam and connect onwards to Trat and Bangkok; for Vietnam the Prek Chak post near Ha Tien is the usual route. Cambodian e-visas should be bought from the official government site before you reach the border, and Vietnamese visas must be arranged in advance. Night buses to Siem Reap take 10-12 hours and are best booked online a day ahead.

intl.to: Koh Rong (Koh Touch) & Koh Rong Sanloem (Saracen Bay, M'Pai Bay) (Cambodia) - from the Serendipity / Ochheuteal pier, 30-45 min
Koh Rong & Koh Rong Sanloem (Cambodia) - from the Serendipity pier

ferry.note: Island ferries leave three or four times a day from the Serendipity pier a short ride from the centre, with several competing companies - Speed Ferry Cambodia and Buva Sea are the main ones - and the crossing to Koh Rong or Koh Rong Sanloem takes 30-45 minutes on a fast catamaran. Departures thin out and can be cancelled outright in the June-October southwest monsoon when the sea gets rough, and the last boat back is usually mid-afternoon. Tickets are open-dated on some companies but the return leg still needs reserving at the island pier. There are no international passenger sailings; Sihanoukville's deep-water port is for containers and cruise calls only.

half.name: Koh Ta Kiev
